info.name: Mosaic realtime - chapter 14
info.description:
The half of chapter 14 that fits in a request and a response.

Decision 43 of Federated GraphQL on .NET says why this collection is smaller than the chapter: newman speaks request and response, and a subscription is a connection that stays open. So the streaming half is scripts/subscription-run.mjs, which both verification scripts call, and this collection covers what is left - which turns out to be most of the chapter's surface.

The write path is here because it was never through the router before: chapters 5 to 13 exercised submitReview against the Reviews subgraph directly, and the plan a mutation gets is a different shape from a query's.

The two subscription fields are here as schema, not as streams. What a request can prove about them is that the graph declares both, that they are routed to different places, and that one of them belongs to a subgraph with no service behind it.

Start the graph before running it:

    docker compose up -d --build mosaic-db mosaic-nats mosaic-catalog \
        mosaic-pricing mosaic-inventory mosaic-accounts mosaic-reviews \
        mosaic-ordering mosaic-nodes mosaic-router

One request writes a review, so a second run against the same database submits a second one. Both are accepted, because they are by different customers.

item.name: Find a product and a customer who has not reviewed it

exec: // Mosaic has no root field listing customers, so the only route to
// one is through somebody's review. Chapter 19 owes the workbook a
// deterministic route; this is the one the gate uses too.
pm.test("there is a customer left who can review the first product", function () {

body.raw: {"query":"{ browseProducts(first: 6) { nodes { id reviews(first: 20) { nodes { author { id } } } } } }"}

item.name: The graph declares two subscriptions, built opposite ways

exec: // Chapter 5 built the first of these and chapter 14 added the
// second. They answer the same question and share no machinery:
// onReviewAdded is a field of the Reviews service, reviewPublished
// is a field of schema/streams.graphql, which has no service.
pm.test("the router serves both subscription fields", function () {
// Both return the same type, which is what makes the comparison
// fair: a client cannot tell from the schema which one is held
// open against a subgraph and which one is a broker subject.
pm.test("both return Review and take a product identifier", function () {

body.raw: {"query":"{ __schema { subscriptionType { fields { name args { name } type { ofType { name } } } } } }"}

item.name: The subgraph knows about only one of them

exec: // The same introspection against the service rather than the
// graph. This is where the two arrangements stop looking alike:
// Reviews implements onReviewAdded and has never heard of
pm.test("Reviews has never heard of reviewPublished", function () {

item.name: A subscription plans to a trigger and a fetch

exec: // Chapters 7 and 10 to 13 read plans made of Single, Parallel and
// Entity nodes. A subscription introduces a node kind none of
// them saw: the trigger is the part that happens once, and every
// child of it happens again on every event.
pm.test("the plan has a trigger", function () {
// The trigger asks the subgraph for the author's key and nothing
// else, because Reviews has a two-field stub for Customer. The
// display name is a second fetch, and it is a child of the
pm.test("the trigger asks only for the author's key", function () {
pm.test("the display name is an entity fetch that depends on the trigger", function () {

body.raw: {"query":"subscription($id: ID!) { onReviewAdded(productId: $id) { id rating author { displayName } } }","variables":{"id":"{{productId}}"}}

item.name: The event-driven subscription plans the same way

exec: // The subgraph name is the finding. Every other trigger and fetch
// in this book names a subgraph out of federation/mosaic.yaml;
// this one names a datasource index and a provider, because there
pm.test("the trigger is not a service", function () {
// Two entity fetches rather than one, and the first is the whole
// point: the broker message carries a type name and a key, so even
// the rating has to be fetched from Reviews.
pm.test("the review itself is fetched by key from Reviews", function () {

body.raw: {"query":"subscription($id: ID!) { reviewPublished(productId: $id) { id rating author { displayName } } }","variables":{"id":"{{productId}}"}}

item.name: A mutation, through the router for the first time

exec: // The write goes to Reviews and the author's name comes from
// Accounts, so the payload of a mutation is resolved across a
// boundary exactly like the payload of a query. Chapters 5 to 13
// sent this mutation to the Reviews subgraph directly, where this
pm.test("the payload resolved the author from another subgraph", function () {

body.raw: {"query":"mutation($p: ID!, $c: ID!) { submitReview(input: { productId: $p, customerId: $c, rating: 5, body: \"Submitted through the router.\" }) { review { id rating author { displayName } } errors { __typename } } }","variables":{"p":"{{productId}}","c":"{{customerId}}"}}

item.name: The review the subscriptions announced is really there

exec: // Chapter 13's node field, used here to close the loop: the
// identifier the mutation returned is the one the broker message
// carried and the one both subscription payloads reported, and it
pm.test("the identifier resolves to a Review", function () {

body.raw: {"query":"query($id: ID!) { node(id: $id) { __typename ... on Review { rating author { displayName } } } }","variables":{"id":"{{submittedReviewId}}"}}
